title: More antidotes: fomepizole, protamine, digoxin Fab, hydroxocobalamin, methylene blue and glucagon
ariaLabel: Schematic of six poisonings and the antidote that acts on each: toxic alcohols are turned into toxic acids by alcohol dehydrogenase, which fomepizole blocks; heparin's anticoagulant effect is neutralised by protamine; digoxin is bound by digoxin antibody fragments; cyanide stops cell respiration and hydroxocobalamin binds it; methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen and methylene blue reduces it back; and beta-blocker overdose lowers cyclic AMP which glucagon restores.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes here, with the effects shown at the cholesterol and the LDL receptors.

nodes.label: Methanol or glycol
nodes.info: Methanol and ethylene glycol are only mildly toxic until they are broken down.

nodes.label: Toxic acids
nodes.info: Acids that cause acidosis, blindness and kidney injury.

nodes.label: Digoxin
nodes.info: Digoxin bound to the sodium-potassium pump.

nodes.label: Digoxin toxicity
nodes.info: Arrhythmia and raised potassium from digoxin.

nodes.label: Cyanide
nodes.info: Cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase so cells cannot use oxygen.

nodes.label: Cell asphyxia
nodes.info: Cells starve for oxygen despite normal blood oxygen.

nodes.label: Methaemoglobin
nodes.info: Haemoglobin with oxidised iron cannot carry oxygen.

nodes.label: Oxygen carrying lost
nodes.info: Blue-brown skin and low oxygen carrying.

nodes.label: Beta-blocker overdose
nodes.info: An overdose of a beta-blocker lowers cAMP in the heart.

nodes.label: Heart failure effect
nodes.info: Slow heart rate and low pressure from low cAMP.

nodes.label: Poisoning effect
nodes.info: A teaching score for the harm done by the poison. The figure shows six separate poisonings side by side, and each antidote reverses only its own.

edges.label: alcohol dehydrogenase
edges.info: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so the toxic acids (formic acid, glycolate and oxalate) are not made. Ethanol competes for the same enzyme and was used before.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: heparin binding
edges.info: Protamine is a positively charged protein that binds the negatively charged heparin and cancels it. It neutralises unfractionated heparin fully and low molecular weight heparin only partly.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: digoxin binding
edges.info: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) bind free digoxin and carry it out in urine. They are used for serious arrhythmia from digoxin toxicity.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: cyanide binding
edges.info: Hydroxocobalamin (vitamin B12a) binds cyanide to make cyanocobalamin, which is passed out in urine. Sodium nitrite and thiosulphate are alternatives.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: reduction of iron
edges.info: Methylene blue is reduced in red cells and then reduces methaemoglobin back to haemoglobin. It is avoided in G6PD deficiency.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

edges.label: glucagon receptor
edges.info: Glucagon raises cAMP through its own receptor, bypassing the blocked beta receptors, and raises heart rate and force.
Adds to the effect shown at the right.

sources: Where each class acts. Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, protamine neutralises heparin, digoxin Fab binds digoxin, hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide, methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin, and glucagon raises cAMP in beta-blocker overdose. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Naloxone, acetylcysteine, atropine with pralidoxime and vitamin K (own figure), flumazenil, activated charcoal, dialysis, timing, supportive care, poison centre advice and doses are left out. Poisoning effect is drawn as a teaching score. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
